Below is a synthesis of what “character functional consistency across a video game narrative” means, why it matters, how it is achieved, and how to evaluate it. Functional consistency refers to a character’s narrative role and behavioral traits remaining coherent—both internally and with audience expectations—across scenes, sessions, and branching story paths so that players can form stable mental models, maintain immersion, and reliably reason about goals and consequences.

# Why functional consistency matters

Players build expectations about non-player characters (NPCs) from the correspondence between appearance and behavior and from how design cues are maintained over time; coherent, consistent design reinforces expectations and improves immersion and decision-making, whereas inconsistent or incoherent design creates uncertainty and stress responses that undermine engagement and perceived intelligence and believability of characters in-game <cite id="8c468f57-2">Players form expectations about NPCs based on the coherence between their appearance and behaviors, and consistency of design over time reinforces expectations and role communication</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent and consistent design reinforced expectations and improved decision-making and ratings of perceived intelligence and believability; inconsistent designs increased uncertainty and stress responses</cite>. Design errors in character appearance–behavior alignment or behavioral logic cause cognitive dissonance and break immersion, directly reducing gameplay quality and user loyalty in competitive markets <cite id="8c468f57-4">Errors such as inappropriate animations, weak AI, or visual inconsistencies degrade gameplay quality and cause cognitive dissonance, breaking immersion and reducing user loyalty</cite>.

# Player perception and expectation: empirical evidence

Experimental work in a military shooter context shows that violating coherence and consistency between appearance and behavior reduces perceived intelligence and believability, while maintaining coherence across multiple interactions supports adaptive expectations and better player performance under pressure; conversely, sustained inconsistency prevents expectation formation and elevates stress <cite id="8c468f57-1">Two experiments in a military shooter examined how coherence and consistency influence perceived intelligence and believability and how breaking expectations affects evaluation and experience</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-0">Decreasing coherence via expectation violations decreases evaluations of NPC design and game experience; experiments measured perceived intelligence and believability across initial interactions and multiple sessions</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent-consistent design reinforced expectations and improved ratings; inconsistent design created uncertainty and increased skin conductance responses (stress)</cite>. These results generalize the classic dramaturgical principle that audiences punish instability in role performance with dramatic irony; in video games, stability in role signals (appearance, speech, behavior patterns) functions as affordances for prediction and plan-making, while violations are deliberately used to create tension or reframe worldviews with costs to immersion if overused <cite id="8c468f57-2">Coherence aligns features with player stereotypes so behaviors fit the wider world; consistency aligns appearance and behavior over time to convey narrative roles</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Reinforcing expectations via coherence/consistency improves decision-making and ratings, while inconsistency undermines them</cite>.

# Modeling and enforcing functional consistency

Architectural patterns for interactive narratives increasingly formalize “character role” as a set of traits, functions, and constraints that must be respected across dialogues, goals, and relationships. In interactive systems built on LLMs, authors inject high-level narrative criteria and use memory/validation modules to keep character behavior aligned with role traits, world state, and authored goals; this addresses free-form input risks that otherwise let generation drift out of scope or violate prior agreements <cite id="085470dd-2">PANGeA uses LLMs for procedural narrative generation in RPGs with a custom memory (Atkinson–Shiffrin) and a novel validation system; designers inject high-level criteria, enabling cohesive, evolving narrative under player input</cite>. Similarly, dynamic role-playing prompts for open-ended RPGs maintain functional consistency by updating each NPC’s prompt bundle with static role information, task context, and current narrative state, and by evaluating alignment with traits, task accuracy, background consistency, and task relevance to chapter goals <cite id="8e10fd44-0">A UGC RPG system dynamically updates NPCs’ role-playing prompts with static info, tasks, and current context; evaluation metrics include alignment with character traits, task accuracy, consistency with background/narrative, and task relevance to chapter goals, sustaining immersion and engagement</cite>.

Ontology-driven approaches provide shared semantic schemas for character roles, relationships, and histories, enabling coherent cross-medium and cross-session continuity. For example, transmedia game ontologies (e.g., OWL-based) structure character knowledge to preserve role coherence as narratives extend across books, comics, and games; in open-world games, dynamic narration adapts to player pathways, yet relies on semantic organization to keep roles and event kernels consistent across many threads <cite id="085470dd-1">An OWL ontology for transmedia narration is used to represent and organize knowledge to create coherent, enriched experiences across media; open-world games evolve to incorporate dynamic narration that enhances immersion while preserving coherence</cite>. Semantic Web techniques can aggregate social-media-derived character information into game character knowledge graphs that support generating consistent character models and enriching narratives beyond manual authoring alone <cite id="085470dd-3">Social media contains rich, unstructured character info; semantic techniques and a Game Character Ontology enable semantically enriched character models and knowledge graphs for generating consistent characters and narratives</cite>.

# Dynamic and branching narratives: preserving roles across paths

Branching systems (state machines, storylets, flowcharts) let authors encode role-preserving transitions among many storylines; maintaining authorial intent across branches requires that role constraints be explicit and enforced, often through modular authoring and play-time validation <cite id="8e10fd44-4">IN authoring tools organize narrative spaces in explicit branching (flowcharts, state machines, storylets), preserving author intent; play-time generation reduces manual effort but demands alternative forms of specification and enforcement</cite>. Contemporary AI-bridged interactive narratives shift authoring to abstract intent prompts while relying on just-in-time generation to adapt to world state; to preserve functional consistency, authors specify beat-level constraints and relationships so that LLMs produce character actions and dialogues that adhere to roles and overarching structures even with emergent variation <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN lets authors express narrative intent abstractly; LLMs render concrete instances at play-time while adhering to an overall structure, enabling emergent narrative under player agency</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-2">WHAT-IF generates controllable branching narratives from a human-written plot, creating choice points via LLM-generated sub-goals and maintaining thematic consistency across many possible endings with structured event tracking</cite>. In commercial LLM-driven characters (e.g., Inworld Origin), characters respond to players with unscripted actions and dialogues that remain aligned to story goals and constraints, demonstrating that functional consistency can be sustained in emergent interactions by tightly coupling generation to world state and author-specified roles <cite id="8e10fd44-3">Inworld Origin features LLM-driven characters that generate unscripted actions and dialogs while adhering to an overall narrative structure</cite>.

# Open-world and long-form RPGs: consistency across emergent play

Open-world games distribute narrative agency across loosely coupled quests, companions, and towns, where character roles (ally/enemy, mentor/foe, class archetype) must persist under player-led discovery and moral choices. Systems that maintain character functional consistency in such settings combine: (a) persistent character models with role traits, goals, and relationship states; (b) dynamic task/context integration so NPCs’ offers and responses remain appropriate to the chapter and world state; and (c) validation/metrics that check trait alignment, background consistency, and task relevance as play unfolds <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic role-playing prompts integrate static role info with current narrative context and tasks; evaluation metrics include alignment with traits, accuracy of information, consistency with background, and relevance to chapter goals to sustain immersion</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-1">PANGeA’s structured memory/validation and engine plug-in maintain cohesive, evolving narratives in turn-based RPGs under player-driven input</cite>. This approach parallels interactive fiction and branching systems: define role- and relationship-level constraints, provide just-in-time scaffolding to player agency, and preserve “narrative kernels” (core functions/events) that keep the world legible across nonlinear exploration <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Branching authoring techniques preserve author intent over complex narrative spaces but face scalability limits; play-time generation reduces burden while demanding structured specifications</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">Abstract narrative specifications transform to concrete instances at play-time to maintain structure amid emergent player influence</cite>.

# Evaluation and metrics for functional consistency

Empirical evaluation ties consistency to player-reported and physiological outcomes: perceived intelligence, believability, decision quality, and stress levels change predictably with coherence/consistency, offering quantitative feedback loops for design and algorithmic validation <cite id="8c468f57-3">Experiments measured perceived intelligence and believability with questionnaires, behavior, and skin conductance; coherent/consistent designs improved ratings and decision-making, while inconsistent designs increased stress</cite>. For algorithmic systems, developers can instrument alignment metrics between generated NPC responses and character trait/role profiles, accuracy of task/goal progress, consistency checks against background knowledge and prior narrative states, and relevance of NPC tasks and dialogues to current chapter objectives to flag drift and maintain immersion at runtime <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Evaluation metrics include alignment with character traits, task execution accuracy, consistency with backgrounds/narratives, and relevance of tasks to current chapter goals</cite> <cite id="085470dd-2">A validation system within PANGeA enforces cohesion and author intent as narratives evolve</cite>. In transmedia and open-world contexts, semantic ontologies can be used to detect contradictions in role inheritance, relationship facts, and event kernels across media and sessions, supporting continuous consistency audits for complex franchises <cite id="085470dd-1">OWL ontologies for transmedia narration enable coherent integration across media and support structured consistency of character knowledge and narrative goals</cite>.

# Practical guidelines and trade-offs

- Anchor roles early: Define appearance–behavior coherence to signal roles (ally/enemy, class archetype), then reinforce consistency of speech patterns, goals, and moral alignment across scenes and sessions so players can form and act on stable mental models <cite id="8c468f57-2">Appearance-behavior coherence and consistency over time communicate roles and reinforce expectations, enabling players to predict behavior and immerse</cite>.
- Use semantic scaffolds: Employ ontologies and character knowledge graphs to encode roles, relationships, and narrative kernels; let these constrain generation and resolve conflicts across media and updates <cite id="085470dd-3">Game Character Ontology and semantic enrichment provide structured character models for consistent generation</cite> <cite id="085470dd-1">Transmedia ontologies preserve coherent character knowledge and experiences across media</cite>.
- Enforce constraints at runtime: Combine memory systems (short-term conversational state, mid-term quest arcs, long-term character development) with validation that checks trait/role adherence, background consistency, and plot-function preservation; expose metrics to authors and live telemetry <cite id="085470dd-2">Custom memory (Atkinson–Shiffrin) plus validation sustains coherent, evolving narratives</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic prompts updated with current context and tasks, evaluated for trait, background, and task-consistency</cite>.
- Design for branching coherence: Author role- and relationship-level constraints rather than scene-by-scene copy; use structured branching (state machines/storylets) or AI-bridged IN with explicit beat-level goals so alternative paths preserve the character’s functional role across endings <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Branching structures (flowcharts, state machines, storylets) preserve author intent but are complex to enumerate exhaustively</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-2">Structured event branching with LLM-generated choice points maintains thematic consistency across many endings</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN adheres to author-specified structures while enabling emergent interactions</cite>.
- Monitor costs of change: Strategic violations can deepen narrative if localized and explained; however, sustained inconsistency reduces perceived intelligence and increases stress, so use such techniques sparingly and with clear payoff <cite id="8c468f57-0">Violating expectations reduces evaluation of NPC design and game experience</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Inconsistent design created uncertainty and elevated stress responses</cite>.

# Summary

Functional consistency is the alignment of a character’s role, traits, and behaviors with audience expectations and internal narrative logic across time and branches. It is empirically tied to higher perceived intelligence and believability, better decision-making, and lower stress; it is computationally enforceable via ontologies, memory/validation systems, and dynamic prompt management; and it is architecturally manageable through structured branching or AI-bridged interactive narratives that preserve role-level constraints while supporting agency. In practice, combining clear role signaling, semantic constraints, runtime validation, and branch-aware authoring yields characters whose functions remain coherent throughout nonlinear, open-ended play, sustaining immersion and engagement <cite id="8c468f57-2">Coherence and consistency communicate roles and expectations, enabling immersion</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent/consistent design boosts perceived intelligence/believability and decision quality, while inconsistency increases stress</cite> <cite id="085470dd-2">Validation and memory architectures keep generated narratives aligned with author intent and character roles</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic role prompts evaluated for trait/background/task consistency sustain immersion in open-ended RPGs</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Authoring with branching structures preserves intent but faces complexity; play-time generation reduces burden with structured specifications</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN adheres to overarching structures to preserve role functionality amid emergent player choices</cite>.

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: N video games, human players control a main character who interacts with non-player characters (NPCs) who populate the game. NPCs are designed with specific characteristics, chosen by game designers, that communicate their role in the narrative. NPCs can play different roles, such as allies or enemies. Game designers often use two characteristics to communicate NPCs' roles in the narrative: appearance and behaviors [1]. Players then form expectations about the role of NPCs based on the perceived coherence between their appearance and their behaviors [2]. Coherence refers to the correspondence between NPCs' features and players' stereotypes. It allows players to understand NPCs' behaviors within the wider context of the game world [3]. Players' expectations are reinforced by the consistency of NPCs' design throughout the game [4]. Consistency refers to the design parameters' alignment, such as appearance and behaviors, over time. It allows players to form expectations and ensure that NPCs' actions match predefined visual cues, in order to convey their role in the game [1]. For example, in a military shooter game, encountering an aggressive NPC who looks like a soldier influences the expectation of hostility when encountering a second NPC with a similar appearance. If the second soldier encountered confirms players' expectations, this will make it easier to predict hostility in subsequent encounters. The aim of maintaining both consistency and coherence between appearance and behaviors is to allow players to form accurate expectations of enemies or allies and, as a result, to improve the overall experience of the game [5]. In particular, when NPCs' behaviors match their appearance and fit logically into the game world, players can better immerse themselves in the narrative and make informed decisions throughout the game. 

As part of their immersion, players form impressions of the NPCs based on their appearance and behaviors [6]. When interacting with NPCs, players assess their perceived intelligence and believability. Perceived intelligence is defined as the player's evaluation of NPCs' abilities to achieve their objective in the narrative, encompassing two dimensions: behaviors' understandability and performance [7].

Experiment 2 focused on the impact of coherence and consistency of NPCs' design on players' game experience. Game experience was analyzed using a combination of questionnaires and behavioral and physiological data. Title: Extracting Semantic-Based Video Game Characters Information from Social Media Platforms
Snippet: Character generation in video games currently relies on game developers manually creating game characters which costs in time, effort and resources. Social media, in the form of blogs, microblogs, forums, wikis, social networks and review sites contain rich information about characters in video games that are not exploited for character generation. However, such information contained in various social media applications are disconnected from one another and are not structured or enriched that can be utilised for character generation. Semantic Web techniques provide ways of linking and enriching information contained in disconnected datasets. This enriched information can be used to build complete character models for generating new characters in video games. Moreover, a video game character knowledge graph can be constructed out of the semantically-enriched information that can be used not only for character generation in video games, but also in any application that requires information about video game characters. In this paper, we present our approach for exploiting social media platforms to create semantically-enriched character models. In particular, we present our Game Character Ontology (GCO) – a light-weight vocabulary for describing character information in video games – and our methodology for extracting and describing (using our ontology) game character information from social media platforms.

Snippet: Video games use interactive storytelling mechanisms that allow players to engage directly with the environment, transforming them into active participants of the game narrative.Static and repetitive interactions with the environmentsuch as with key items, events, and non-playable characters (NPCs)-can negatively impact players experiences and their desire to replay games (Garavaglia et al. 2022).Procedural narrative generation is a widely accepted approach to this problem (Balint and Bidarra 2023;Sandhu and McCoy 2023).Early research on procedural narrative generation primarily focused on creating coherent sequences of events; however, this alone may fail to produce an engaging narrative that responds dynamically to the player (Lin and Riedl 2021).

Title: WHAT-IF: Exploring Branching Narratives by Meta-Prompting Large Language Models
Snippet: Interactive fiction (IF) is a form of text-based story where a user performs some action that moves the plot along. From Choose Your Own Adven-ture™ books to open-world video games, branching narratives are an interesting element of interactive fiction that enables the reader to change the outcome of the narrative. 

In this paper, we present WHAT-IF (Writing a Hero's Alternate Timeline through Interactive Fiction)1 , a system for controllable, branching narrative generation in English. Starting with a humanwritten plot, WHAT-IF produces distinct changes in the plot by considering alternate actions the main character could have taken. We create these choice points by having a large language model (LLM) generate a new sub-goal for the character, which significantly changes subsequent plot points in the story. We use this LLM-driven branching narrative Figure 1: The WHAT-IF user interface, filled with the main character, title, and the plot of the TV show Wan-daVision taken from IMDb. The main character, title, and the plot summary can all be edited by the user. See Appendix A for the output generated using this prompt. 

to create an interactive fiction system (Fig. 1) allowing the user to choose which branches to follow in the story tree. 

In contrast with previous LLM-driven interactive fiction systems like AI Dungeon2 , which rely entirely on the user to move the story along, WHAT-IF generates more constrained stories where the user has a degree of control but the stories generated by the LLM maintain a high degree of thematic consistency with the original story, even with many possible endings. 

Structure can help LLMs better understand stories (Dong et al., 2023). WHAT-IF breaks down the narrative into events so that the structure of the plot can be tracked throughout the generation. A branching plot structure, such as that shown in Fig- ure 2, is generated before the user plays the game. Each branch of the story will lead to an ending. 

As each story requires asking different questions to generate hypothetical alternate plots, we also employ meta-prompting. That is, the system generates story-specific prompts to be fed into another instance of the LLM to answer.

Title: WhatELSE: Shaping Narrative Spaces at Configurable Level of Abstraction for AI-bridged Interactive Storytelling
Snippet: Interactive Narrative (IN) is a form of digital storytelling experience where the player can influence a dramatic storyline through their actions [27,63]. IN takes various forms in entertainment and education applications, with the most prominent one being branching storylines in role-playing games [61], where the author predefines the range of player actions and creates multiple storylines reflecting the consequences of different player choices. Instead of one single narrative, the author creates a narrative space consisting of all possible storylines a player can experience. 

The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has the potential to revolutionize IN by enabling the automatic generation of content based on the user's specifications [42,44,89]. This enables just-in-time generation of narrative content to adapt to different game world states. Instead of enumerating all possible storylines, authors can convey their broad narrative intent to the LLM as prompts, and let the model render concrete narrative instances customized by the player's in-game context [10,36,57,79]. For example, Inworld Origin [2] is a narrative-driven adventure game where the player interacts with LLM-driven characters to solve a mystery. The characters respond to the player with unscripted actions and dialogs that are generated by LLMs at play-time, while still adhering to an overall narrative structure. AI-bridged IN significantly enhances player agency as the player can now influence the story in ways not restricted by predefined story branches, and also facilitates a form of emergent narrative [5,77] where the final narrative experience can even possibly go beyond the author's anticipation. 

To create a traditional IN, the author directly specifies concrete narrative instances conditioned on game world states, while in the case of AI-bridged IN, the author has to express their narrative intent as prompts -which requires them to write abstract narrative specifications. The abstract specification eventually transforms into concrete narrative instances at play-time based on the player's interaction with the game system.
</snippet>

Every possible narrative instance is manually authored, which ensures that the author's intent is precisely preserved [63]. Much of the prior work seeks to make the authoring process more efficient through more compact representations of storylines [69]. However, despite these efforts, the complexity of defining all possible plot progressions remains a significant challenge [63]. IN authoring continues to be a time-intensive and engineering-heavy process, often falling short of expectations [26,71]. 

Recent efforts have moved towards play-time narrative generation, reducing the need for extensive manual authoring [21,23]. Authors set high-level narrative requirements, allowing for automated procedural story generation that responds to player actions [64]. While this approach saves manual effort, authors need to express their authorial intent through means other than high-level specifications. To address this challenge, our system proposes various levels of abstraction grounded in the theory of narrative structure [50], allowing authors to express design requirements from beat-level concrete details to story-level flexible goals.

Below is a synthesis of what “character functional consistency across a video game narrative” means, why it matters, how it is achieved, and how to evaluate it. Functional consistency refers to a character’s narrative role and behavioral traits remaining coherent—both internally and with audience expectations—across scenes, sessions, and branching story paths so that players can form stable mental models, maintain immersion, and reliably reason about goals and consequences.

# Why functional consistency matters

Players build expectations about non-player characters (NPCs) from the correspondence between appearance and behavior and from how design cues are maintained over time; coherent, consistent design reinforces expectations and improves immersion and decision-making, whereas inconsistent or incoherent design creates uncertainty and stress responses that undermine engagement and perceived intelligence and believability of characters in-game <cite id="8c468f57-2">Players form expectations about NPCs based on the coherence between their appearance and behaviors, and consistency of design over time reinforces expectations and role communication</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent and consistent design reinforced expectations and improved decision-making and ratings of perceived intelligence and believability; inconsistent designs increased uncertainty and stress responses</cite>. Design errors in character appearance–behavior alignment or behavioral logic cause cognitive dissonance and break immersion, directly reducing gameplay quality and user loyalty in competitive markets <cite id="8c468f57-4">Errors such as inappropriate animations, weak AI, or visual inconsistencies degrade gameplay quality and cause cognitive dissonance, breaking immersion and reducing user loyalty</cite>.

# Player perception and expectation: empirical evidence

Experimental work in a military shooter context shows that violating coherence and consistency between appearance and behavior reduces perceived intelligence and believability, while maintaining coherence across multiple interactions supports adaptive expectations and better player performance under pressure; conversely, sustained inconsistency prevents expectation formation and elevates stress <cite id="8c468f57-1">Two experiments in a military shooter examined how coherence and consistency influence perceived intelligence and believability and how breaking expectations affects evaluation and experience</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-0">Decreasing coherence via expectation violations decreases evaluations of NPC design and game experience; experiments measured perceived intelligence and believability across initial interactions and multiple sessions</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent-consistent design reinforced expectations and improved ratings; inconsistent design created uncertainty and increased skin conductance responses (stress)</cite>. These results generalize the classic dramaturgical principle that audiences punish instability in role performance with dramatic irony; in video games, stability in role signals (appearance, speech, behavior patterns) functions as affordances for prediction and plan-making, while violations are deliberately used to create tension or reframe worldviews with costs to immersion if overused <cite id="8c468f57-2">Coherence aligns features with player stereotypes so behaviors fit the wider world; consistency aligns appearance and behavior over time to convey narrative roles</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Reinforcing expectations via coherence/consistency improves decision-making and ratings, while inconsistency undermines them</cite>.

# Modeling and enforcing functional consistency

Architectural patterns for interactive narratives increasingly formalize “character role” as a set of traits, functions, and constraints that must be respected across dialogues, goals, and relationships. In interactive systems built on LLMs, authors inject high-level narrative criteria and use memory/validation modules to keep character behavior aligned with role traits, world state, and authored goals; this addresses free-form input risks that otherwise let generation drift out of scope or violate prior agreements <cite id="085470dd-2">PANGeA uses LLMs for procedural narrative generation in RPGs with a custom memory (Atkinson–Shiffrin) and a novel validation system; designers inject high-level criteria, enabling cohesive, evolving narrative under player input</cite>. Similarly, dynamic role-playing prompts for open-ended RPGs maintain functional consistency by updating each NPC’s prompt bundle with static role information, task context, and current narrative state, and by evaluating alignment with traits, task accuracy, background consistency, and task relevance to chapter goals <cite id="8e10fd44-0">A UGC RPG system dynamically updates NPCs’ role-playing prompts with static info, tasks, and current context; evaluation metrics include alignment with character traits, task accuracy, consistency with background/narrative, and task relevance to chapter goals, sustaining immersion and engagement</cite>.

Ontology-driven approaches provide shared semantic schemas for character roles, relationships, and histories, enabling coherent cross-medium and cross-session continuity. For example, transmedia game ontologies (e.g., OWL-based) structure character knowledge to preserve role coherence as narratives extend across books, comics, and games; in open-world games, dynamic narration adapts to player pathways, yet relies on semantic organization to keep roles and event kernels consistent across many threads <cite id="085470dd-1">An OWL ontology for transmedia narration is used to represent and organize knowledge to create coherent, enriched experiences across media; open-world games evolve to incorporate dynamic narration that enhances immersion while preserving coherence</cite>. Semantic Web techniques can aggregate social-media-derived character information into game character knowledge graphs that support generating consistent character models and enriching narratives beyond manual authoring alone <cite id="085470dd-3">Social media contains rich, unstructured character info; semantic techniques and a Game Character Ontology enable semantically enriched character models and knowledge graphs for generating consistent characters and narratives</cite>.

# Dynamic and branching narratives: preserving roles across paths

Branching systems (state machines, storylets, flowcharts) let authors encode role-preserving transitions among many storylines; maintaining authorial intent across branches requires that role constraints be explicit and enforced, often through modular authoring and play-time validation <cite id="8e10fd44-4">IN authoring tools organize narrative spaces in explicit branching (flowcharts, state machines, storylets), preserving author intent; play-time generation reduces manual effort but demands alternative forms of specification and enforcement</cite>. Contemporary AI-bridged interactive narratives shift authoring to abstract intent prompts while relying on just-in-time generation to adapt to world state; to preserve functional consistency, authors specify beat-level constraints and relationships so that LLMs produce character actions and dialogues that adhere to roles and overarching structures even with emergent variation <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN lets authors express narrative intent abstractly; LLMs render concrete instances at play-time while adhering to an overall structure, enabling emergent narrative under player agency</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-2">WHAT-IF generates controllable branching narratives from a human-written plot, creating choice points via LLM-generated sub-goals and maintaining thematic consistency across many possible endings with structured event tracking</cite>. In commercial LLM-driven characters (e.g., Inworld Origin), characters respond to players with unscripted actions and dialogues that remain aligned to story goals and constraints, demonstrating that functional consistency can be sustained in emergent interactions by tightly coupling generation to world state and author-specified roles <cite id="8e10fd44-3">Inworld Origin features LLM-driven characters that generate unscripted actions and dialogs while adhering to an overall narrative structure</cite>.

# Open-world and long-form RPGs: consistency across emergent play

Open-world games distribute narrative agency across loosely coupled quests, companions, and towns, where character roles (ally/enemy, mentor/foe, class archetype) must persist under player-led discovery and moral choices. Systems that maintain character functional consistency in such settings combine: (a) persistent character models with role traits, goals, and relationship states; (b) dynamic task/context integration so NPCs’ offers and responses remain appropriate to the chapter and world state; and (c) validation/metrics that check trait alignment, background consistency, and task relevance as play unfolds <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic role-playing prompts integrate static role info with current narrative context and tasks; evaluation metrics include alignment with traits, accuracy of information, consistency with background, and relevance to chapter goals to sustain immersion</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-1">PANGeA’s structured memory/validation and engine plug-in maintain cohesive, evolving narratives in turn-based RPGs under player-driven input</cite>. This approach parallels interactive fiction and branching systems: define role- and relationship-level constraints, provide just-in-time scaffolding to player agency, and preserve “narrative kernels” (core functions/events) that keep the world legible across nonlinear exploration <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Branching authoring techniques preserve author intent over complex narrative spaces but face scalability limits; play-time generation reduces burden while demanding structured specifications</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">Abstract narrative specifications transform to concrete instances at play-time to maintain structure amid emergent player influence</cite>.

# Evaluation and metrics for functional consistency

Empirical evaluation ties consistency to player-reported and physiological outcomes: perceived intelligence, believability, decision quality, and stress levels change predictably with coherence/consistency, offering quantitative feedback loops for design and algorithmic validation <cite id="8c468f57-3">Experiments measured perceived intelligence and believability with questionnaires, behavior, and skin conductance; coherent/consistent designs improved ratings and decision-making, while inconsistent designs increased stress</cite>. For algorithmic systems, developers can instrument alignment metrics between generated NPC responses and character trait/role profiles, accuracy of task/goal progress, consistency checks against background knowledge and prior narrative states, and relevance of NPC tasks and dialogues to current chapter objectives to flag drift and maintain immersion at runtime <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Evaluation metrics include alignment with character traits, task execution accuracy, consistency with backgrounds/narratives, and relevance of tasks to current chapter goals</cite> <cite id="085470dd-2">A validation system within PANGeA enforces cohesion and author intent as narratives evolve</cite>. In transmedia and open-world contexts, semantic ontologies can be used to detect contradictions in role inheritance, relationship facts, and event kernels across media and sessions, supporting continuous consistency audits for complex franchises <cite id="085470dd-1">OWL ontologies for transmedia narration enable coherent integration across media and support structured consistency of character knowledge and narrative goals</cite>.

# Practical guidelines and trade-offs

- Anchor roles early: Define appearance–behavior coherence to signal roles (ally/enemy, class archetype), then reinforce consistency of speech patterns, goals, and moral alignment across scenes and sessions so players can form and act on stable mental models <cite id="8c468f57-2">Appearance-behavior coherence and consistency over time communicate roles and reinforce expectations, enabling players to predict behavior and immerse</cite>.
- Use semantic scaffolds: Employ ontologies and character knowledge graphs to encode roles, relationships, and narrative kernels; let these constrain generation and resolve conflicts across media and updates <cite id="085470dd-3">Game Character Ontology and semantic enrichment provide structured character models for consistent generation</cite> <cite id="085470dd-1">Transmedia ontologies preserve coherent character knowledge and experiences across media</cite>.
- Enforce constraints at runtime: Combine memory systems (short-term conversational state, mid-term quest arcs, long-term character development) with validation that checks trait/role adherence, background consistency, and plot-function preservation; expose metrics to authors and live telemetry <cite id="085470dd-2">Custom memory (Atkinson–Shiffrin) plus validation sustains coherent, evolving narratives</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic prompts updated with current context and tasks, evaluated for trait, background, and task-consistency</cite>.
- Design for branching coherence: Author role- and relationship-level constraints rather than scene-by-scene copy; use structured branching (state machines/storylets) or AI-bridged IN with explicit beat-level goals so alternative paths preserve the character’s functional role across endings <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Branching structures (flowcharts, state machines, storylets) preserve author intent but are complex to enumerate exhaustively</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-2">Structured event branching with LLM-generated choice points maintains thematic consistency across many endings</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN adheres to author-specified structures while enabling emergent interactions</cite>.
- Monitor costs of change: Strategic violations can deepen narrative if localized and explained; however, sustained inconsistency reduces perceived intelligence and increases stress, so use such techniques sparingly and with clear payoff <cite id="8c468f57-0">Violating expectations reduces evaluation of NPC design and game experience</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Inconsistent design created uncertainty and elevated stress responses</cite>.

# Summary

Functional consistency is the alignment of a character’s role, traits, and behaviors with audience expectations and internal narrative logic across time and branches. It is empirically tied to higher perceived intelligence and believability, better decision-making, and lower stress; it is computationally enforceable via ontologies, memory/validation systems, and dynamic prompt management; and it is architecturally manageable through structured branching or AI-bridged interactive narratives that preserve role-level constraints while supporting agency. In practice, combining clear role signaling, semantic constraints, runtime validation, and branch-aware authoring yields characters whose functions remain coherent throughout nonlinear, open-ended play, sustaining immersion and engagement <cite id="8c468f57-2">Coherence and consistency communicate roles and expectations, enabling immersion</cite> <cite id="8c468f57-3">Coherent/consistent design boosts perceived intelligence/believability and decision quality, while inconsistency increases stress</cite> <cite id="085470dd-2">Validation and memory architectures keep generated narratives aligned with author intent and character roles</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-0">Dynamic role prompts evaluated for trait/background/task consistency sustain immersion in open-ended RPGs</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-4">Authoring with branching structures preserves intent but faces complexity; play-time generation reduces burden with structured specifications</cite> <cite id="8e10fd44-3">AI-bridged IN adheres to overarching structures to preserve role functionality amid emergent player choices</cite>.</answer>

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: In video games, non-player characters (NPCs) have an essential role in shaping players' experiences. The design of their appearance and their behaviors can be manipulated in coherence and consistency to maintain players' expectations or on the contrary to induce surprise. The influence of NPCs’ coherence and consistency on players’ evaluation of them remains to be unveiled. To fill this gap, two experiments were conducted in the context of a military shooter game. Players’ evaluation of NPCs’ perceived intelligence and believability, were measured, as these two dimensions are fundamental for their adoption and engagement toward them. The first experiment investigated the impact of breaking players' initial expectations on the evaluation of NPCs. The second experiment focused on the influence of NPCs’ coherence and consistency on both players' expectations and evaluation of NPCs, by means of a combination of questionnaires, behavioral, and physiological measures. Our results reveal that breaking players' expectations influence their evaluation of NPCs, with coherent and consistent design reinforcing expectations and incoherent design challenging them.

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: N video games, human players control a main character who interacts with non-player characters (NPCs) who populate the game. NPCs are designed with specific characteristics, chosen by game designers, that communicate their role in the narrative. NPCs can play different roles, such as allies or enemies. Game designers often use two characteristics to communicate NPCs' roles in the narrative: appearance and behaviors [1]. Players then form expectations about the role of NPCs based on the perceived coherence between their appearance and their behaviors [2]. Coherence refers to the correspondence between NPCs' features and players' stereotypes. It allows players to understand NPCs' behaviors within the wider context of the game world [3]. Players' expectations are reinforced by the consistency of NPCs' design throughout the game [4]. Consistency refers to the design parameters' alignment, such as appearance and behaviors, over time. It allows players to form expectations and ensure that NPCs' actions match predefined visual cues, in order to convey their role in the game [1]. For example, in a military shooter game, encountering an aggressive NPC who looks like a soldier influences the expectation of hostility when encountering a second NPC with a similar appearance. If the second soldier encountered confirms players' expectations, this will make it easier to predict hostility in subsequent encounters. The aim of maintaining both consistency and coherence between appearance and behaviors is to allow players to form accurate expectations of enemies or allies and, as a result, to improve the overall experience of the game [5]. In particular, when NPCs' behaviors match their appearance and fit logically into the game world, players can better immerse themselves in the narrative and make informed decisions throughout the game. 

As part of their immersion, players form impressions of the NPCs based on their appearance and behaviors [6]. When interacting with NPCs, players assess their perceived intelligence and believability. Perceived intelligence is defined as the player's evaluation of NPCs' abilities to achieve their objective in the narrative, encompassing two dimensions: behaviors' understandability and performance [7].

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: This study investigated the influence of NPCs' design (coherence and consistency) on players' expectations and ratings of perceived intelligence and believability. Experiment 1 revealed the consequences of violating players' expectations regarding NPCs' appearance and behaviors. Because players rely on their knowledge and prior experiences to form expectations, violating these expectations negatively affects their assessment of NPCs' abilities to achieve their purpose in the narrative. Experiment 2 focused on the impact of coherence and consistency of NPCs' design on players' game experience. Game experience was analyzed using a combination of questionnaires and behavioral and physiological data. First, the coherent and consistent design of NPCs reinforced players' expectations, leading to improved decision-making and ratings of NPCs' perceived intelligence and believability. Second, incoherent and consistent NPCs challenged players' expectations, but they were able to adjust their expectations over time. Third, inconsistent NPCs' design created uncertainty and prevented participants from forming accurate expectations, leading to increased stress as measured by the amplitude of their skin conductance responses. Overall, our study offers insights into the complex interplay between NPC design, player expectations, and their ratings of perceived intelligence and believability. These findings underscore the potential for game designers to create alternative game experiences by strategically manipulating players' expectations or by maintaining coherence and consistency in NPCs' design. In conclusion, a more profound comprehension of the impact of coherence and consistency on players' expectations can assist in the future design of more engaging and immersive player experiences.

Title: Essential Principles of Video Game Character Design: Impact of Bugs on Gameplay and User Engagement
Snippet: Character design for video games is a process that requires consideration of multiple aspects, such as visual aesthetics, behavioral patterns, animations, and sound effects. Characters in gameplay form the foundation of the narrative element, creating an emotional connection with the player and influencing their perception and immersion in the game world. This aspect of game development is especially relevant in the competitive video game market. 

The importance of this topic is underscored by the fact that errors in character design-such as inappropriate animations, weak AI, or visual inconsistencies-significantly degrade gameplay quality and cause cognitive dissonance for the user. Poorly developed characters break immersion, leading to a loss of interest and reduced user loyalty. Attention to detail in character design has become a necessary aspect of video game development, determining the product's success and competitiveness in the market. 

The purpose of this study is to analyze the main principles of character design for video games and examine how design errors impact gameplay and user perception.

Character design for video games is a process that requires consideration of multiple aspects, such as visual aesthetics, behavioral patterns, animations, and sound effects. Characters in gameplay form the foundation of the narrative element, creating an emotional connection with the player and influencing their perception and immersion in the game world. This aspect of game development is especially relevant in the competitive video game market. 

The importance of this topic is underscored by the fact that errors in character design-such as inappropriate animations, weak AI, or visual inconsistencies-significantly degrade gameplay quality and cause cognitive dissonance for the user. Poorly developed characters break immersion, leading to a loss of interest and reduced user loyalty. Attention to detail in character design has become a necessary aspect of video game development, determining the product's success and competitiveness in the market. 

The purpose of this study is to analyze the main principles of character design for video games and examine how design errors impact gameplay and user perception.

Title: Extracting Semantic-Based Video Game Characters Information from Social Media Platforms
Snippet: Character generation in video games currently relies on game developers manually creating game characters which costs in time, effort and resources. Semantic Web techniques provide ways of linking and enriching information contained in disconnected datasets. This enriched information can be used to build complete character models for generating new characters in video games. Moreover, a video game character knowledge graph can be constructed out of the semantically-enriched information that can be used not only for character generation in video games, but also in any application that requires information about video game characters. In particular, we present our Game Character Ontology (GCO) – a light-weight vocabulary for describing character information in video games – and our methodology for extracting and describing (using our ontology) game character information from social media platforms.

documents.snippet:
Video games use interactive storytelling mechanisms that allow players to engage directly with the environment, transforming them into active participants of the game narrative.Static and repetitive interactions with the environmentsuch as with key items, events, and non-playable characters (NPCs)-can negatively impact players experiences and their desire to replay games (Garavaglia et al. 2022).Procedural narrative generation is a widely accepted approach to this problem (Balint and Bidarra 2023;Sandhu and McCoy 2023).Early research on procedural narrative generation primarily focused on creating coherent sequences of events; however, this alone may fail to produce an engaging narrative that responds dynamically to the player (Lin and Riedl 2021).

Large language models (LLMs) offer unprecedented flexibility in procedural generation, enabling the creation of dynamic video game storylines that can evolve with user input (Inworld AI 2024;Kumaran et al. 2023;Mori 2023;Nimpattanavong et al. 2023;Sun et al. 2023).Enabling players and developers to provide dynamic or free-form text input to drive generation is a critical aspect of realizing the greater potential of LLMs.However, ingesting free-form text for a video game poses challenges.Dynamic text input can prompt the LLM to generate content beyond the narrative scope, making it difficult to encourage user agency while maintaining a cohesive, evolving narrative (Kumaran et al. 2023; Uludag˘lı and Og˘uz 2023; Lin and Riedl 2021).

Given these challenges, this research introduces PANGeA, standing for Procedural Artificial Narrative using Generative AI.PANGeA is a structured approach that uses LLMs for the procedural generation of interactive narratives in turn-based role-playing games (RPGs).PANGeA is comprised of components including a custom memory system (based on the Atkinson-Shiffrin model), a novel validation system, a Unity game engine plug-in, and a server with a RESTful interface that enables connecting PANGeA components with any game engine as well as local and private LLMs.PANGeA's approach to narrative generation drives game development as well as gameplay.During development a game designer injects high-level narrative criteria into PANGeA's prompt schema.

documents.title: Extracting Semantic-Based Video Game Characters Information from Social Media Platforms
documents.snippet: Character generation in video games currently relies on game developers manually creating game characters which costs in time, effort and resources. Social media, in the form of blogs, microblogs, forums, wikis, social networks and review sites contain rich information about characters in video games that are not exploited for character generation. However, such information contained in various social media applications are disconnected from one another and are not structured or enriched that can be utilised for character generation. Semantic Web techniques provide ways of linking and enriching information contained in disconnected datasets. This enriched information can be used to build complete character models for generating new characters in video games. Moreover, a video game character knowledge graph can be constructed out of the semantically-enriched information that can be used not only for character generation in video games, but also in any application that requires information about video game characters. In this paper, we present our approach for exploiting social media platforms to create semantically-enriched character models. In particular, we present our Game Character Ontology (GCO) – a light-weight vocabulary for describing character information in video games – and our methodology for extracting and describing (using our ontology) game character information from social media platforms.

For objects this implies a scale of objects from something that may only be observed to exist under the non-interactable category, to something that can be invented in the game, by for example using programing code available inside the game interface under the inventible category. Title: WHAT-IF: Exploring Branching Narratives by Meta-Prompting Large Language Models
Snippet: Interactive fiction (IF) is a form of text-based story where a user performs some action that moves the plot along. From Choose Your Own Adven-ture™ books to open-world video games, branching narratives are an interesting element of interactive fiction that enables the reader to change the outcome of the narrative. 

In this paper, we present WHAT-IF (Writing a Hero's Alternate Timeline through Interactive Fiction)1 , a system for controllable, branching narrative generation in English. Starting with a humanwritten plot, WHAT-IF produces distinct changes in the plot by considering alternate actions the main character could have taken. We create these choice points by having a large language model (LLM) generate a new sub-goal for the character, which significantly changes subsequent plot points in the story. We use this LLM-driven branching narrative Figure 1: The WHAT-IF user interface, filled with the main character, title, and the plot of the TV show Wan-daVision taken from IMDb. The main character, title, and the plot summary can all be edited by the user. See Appendix A for the output generated using this prompt. 

to create an interactive fiction system (Fig. 1) allowing the user to choose which branches to follow in the story tree. 

In contrast with previous LLM-driven interactive fiction systems like AI Dungeon2 , which rely entirely on the user to move the story along, WHAT-IF generates more constrained stories where the user has a degree of control but the stories generated by the LLM maintain a high degree of thematic consistency with the original story, even with many possible endings. 

Structure can help LLMs better understand stories (Dong et al., 2023). WHAT-IF breaks down the narrative into events so that the structure of the plot can be tracked throughout the generation. A branching plot structure, such as that shown in Fig- ure 2, is generated before the user plays the game. Each branch of the story will lead to an ending.

Title: WhatELSE: Shaping Narrative Spaces at Configurable Level of Abstraction for AI-bridged Interactive Storytelling
Snippet: Interactive Narrative (IN) is a form of digital storytelling experience where the player can influence a dramatic storyline through their actions [27,63]. IN takes various forms in entertainment and education applications, with the most prominent one being branching storylines in role-playing games [61], where the author predefines the range of player actions and creates multiple storylines reflecting the consequences of different player choices. Instead of one single narrative, the author creates a narrative space consisting of all possible storylines a player can experience. 

The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has the potential to revolutionize IN by enabling the automatic generation of content based on the user's specifications [42,44,89]. This enables just-in-time generation of narrative content to adapt to different game world states. Instead of enumerating all possible storylines, authors can convey their broad narrative intent to the LLM as prompts, and let the model render concrete narrative instances customized by the player's in-game context [10,36,57,79]. For example, Inworld Origin [2] is a narrative-driven adventure game where the player interacts with LLM-driven characters to solve a mystery. The characters respond to the player with unscripted actions and dialogs that are generated by LLMs at play-time, while still adhering to an overall narrative structure. AI-bridged IN significantly enhances player agency as the player can now influence the story in ways not restricted by predefined story branches, and also facilitates a form of emergent narrative [5,77] where the final narrative experience can even possibly go beyond the author's anticipation. 

To create a traditional IN, the author directly specifies concrete narrative instances conditioned on game world states, while in the case of AI-bridged IN, the author has to express their narrative intent as prompts -which requires them to write abstract narrative specifications. The abstract specification eventually transforms into concrete narrative instances at play-time based on the player's interaction with the game system.

Title: WhatELSE: Shaping Narrative Spaces at Configurable Level of Abstraction for AI-bridged Interactive Storytelling
Snippet: Various tools have been proposed to support authoring Interactive Narratives (IN) in the past decades [25,26,67]. Many of these tools are designed to give better control and management over branching storylines, enabling rich player actions while maintaining authorial control [22]. IN Authoring tools usually organize the narrative space in explicit branching structure [13] to enable intuitive understanding, including flowchart-like structures [22], state machines [24,80], and collections of modular story chunks conditioned on game world states ("storylet") [38]. Every possible narrative instance is manually authored, which ensures that the author's intent is precisely preserved [63]. Much of the prior work seeks to make the authoring process more efficient through more compact representations of storylines [69]. However, despite these efforts, the complexity of defining all possible plot progressions remains a significant challenge [63]. IN authoring continues to be a time-intensive and engineering-heavy process, often falling short of expectations [26,71]. 

Recent efforts have moved towards play-time narrative generation, reducing the need for extensive manual authoring [21,23]. Authors set high-level narrative requirements, allowing for automated procedural story generation that responds to player actions [64]. While this approach saves manual effort, authors need to express their authorial intent through means other than high-level specifications. To address this challenge, our system proposes various levels of abstraction grounded in the theory of narrative structure [50], allowing authors to express design requirements from beat-level concrete details to story-level flexible goals.

IN takes various forms in entertainment and education applications, with the most prominent one being branching storylines in role-playing games [61], where the author predefines the range of player actions and creates multiple storylines reflecting the consequences of different player choices. Instead of one single narrative, the author creates a narrative space consisting of all possible storylines a player can experience. 

The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has the potential to revolutionize IN by enabling the automatic generation of content based on the user's specifications [42,44,89]. This enables just-in-time generation of narrative content to adapt to different game world states. Instead of enumerating all possible storylines, authors can convey their broad narrative intent to the LLM as prompts, and let the model render concrete narrative instances customized by the player's in-game context [10,36,57,79]. For example, Inworld Origin [2] is a narrative-driven adventure game where the player interacts with LLM-driven characters to solve a mystery. The characters respond to the player with unscripted actions and dialogs that are generated by LLMs at play-time, while still adhering to an overall narrative structure. AI-bridged IN significantly enhances player agency as the player can now influence the story in ways not restricted by predefined story branches, and also facilitates a form of emergent narrative [5,77] where the final narrative experience can even possibly go beyond the author's anticipation. 

To create a traditional IN, the author directly specifies concrete narrative instances conditioned on game world states, while in the case of AI-bridged IN, the author has to express their narrative intent as prompts -which requires them to write abstract narrative specifications. The abstract specification eventually transforms into concrete narrative instances at play-time based on the player's interaction with the game system.

documents.snippet:
Various tools have been proposed to support authoring Interactive Narratives (IN) in the past decades [25,26,67]. Many of these tools are designed to give better control and management over branching storylines, enabling rich player actions while maintaining authorial control [22]. IN Authoring tools usually organize the narrative space in explicit branching structure [13] to enable intuitive understanding, including flowchart-like structures [22], state machines [24,80], and collections of modular story chunks conditioned on game world states ("storylet") [38]. Every possible narrative instance is manually authored, which ensures that the author's intent is precisely preserved [63]. Much of the prior work seeks to make the authoring process more efficient through more compact representations of storylines [69]. However, despite these efforts, the complexity of defining all possible plot progressions remains a significant challenge [63]. IN authoring continues to be a time-intensive and engineering-heavy process, often falling short of expectations [26,71]. 

Recent efforts have moved towards play-time narrative generation, reducing the need for extensive manual authoring [21,23]. Authors set high-level narrative requirements, allowing for automated procedural story generation that responds to player actions [64]. While this approach saves manual effort, authors need to express their authorial intent through means other than high-level specifications. To address this challenge, our system proposes various levels of abstraction grounded in the theory of narrative structure [50], allowing authors to express design requirements from beat-level concrete details to story-level flexible goals.

Summary
Designers sometimes need to relax character consistency to keep player agency meaningful, but this should be done selectively and with compensatory design so players retain orientation and trust in the world. The literature shows that consistency and coherence build expectations and immersion; agency demands responsiveness and autonomy; and the core tension arises when player actions or goals conflict with a fixed character identity or prior narrative commitments. When trade-offs are necessary, designers can justify inconsistency by directly serving player decisions, maintaining broader story coherence, or aligning with player identification, while mitigating confusion through transparent mechanics, meta-narrative scaffolds, and runtime planning that jointly optimizes persona and plot constraints. <cite id="cee9dd4c-4">NPCs signal roles through appearance and behavior, and players form expectations from their coherence and consistency over time; matching these supports immersion and informed decisions</cite> <cite id="cee9dd4c-0">Character consistency, multi-agent coordination, and plot adherence are core interactive-drama quality axes</cite> <cite id="39de8573-1">Interactive narrative design has long grappled with the tension between linear storytelling and player agency, motivating architectures that accommodate choice</cite> <cite id="39de8573-4">Balancing unrestrained autonomy with controlled plot is an explicit design dilemma; triggerword-controlled progression paired with player exploration is one mitigation</cite> <cite id="e534b49a-1">Believable characters rely on persona consistency, but persona consistency can conflict with narrative coherence; a joint persona-activity planner can resolve such conflicts</cite> <cite id="e534b49a-2">Players vary in how much they project onto a PC and in their tolerance for malleable character images; these differences shape perceived agency and satisfaction despite predefined narratives</cite>.

When character consistency should be preserved (baseline)
- To support expectation formation and orientation: When an NPC’s outward design (appearance), behavior style, and on-screen actions remain coherent and consistent, players can more quickly form accurate mental models, anticipate roles, and make informed decisions. Breaking coherence or consistency at these moments undermines orientation and can frustrate agency if players cannot predict what options are safe or meaningful. <cite id="cee9dd4c-4">Coherence between appearance and behavior and consistency over time help players identify roles, predict hostility or ally behavior, and immerse; these expectations enable informed decisions</cite>.
- To sustain immersion and credibility: Consistent behavior with a character’s goals, knowledge, and constraints sustains transportation and perceived intelligence/believability. Frequent, unannounced contradictions degrade immersion, making player choices feel “exploiting a glitch” rather than engaging meaningfully. <cite id="cee9dd4c-1">Role fidelity—consistent speech and action aligned with assigned roles—supports immersion and gameplay effectiveness; failure (role drift) degrades both</cite>.
- When choices are locally contingent on identity logic: If a player’s success set depends on the character being, say, lawful, paranoid, or honor-bound, violating that logic can nullify decision “stakes.” Preserve consistency to keep consequences isomorphic with identity. <cite id="cee9dd4c-3">Agency metrics include Player Influence (how behavior shifts plot) and Intention Following (how reactions fulfill player intentions); maintaining consistency improves both</cite>.

When to sacrifice consistency to preserve agency
- To keep meaningful choices when the designer’s world model is too brittle: If a player’s autonomous choice creates a dead end that a rigidly consistent NPC would escalate (e.g., an honor-bound NPC reports a betrayal to the wrong party, dooming the party), bend the NPC’s rule to let the player’s intent succeed. This preserves the perceived agency that narrative mechanics are supposed to serve. <cite id="39de8573-1">Early interactive narrative work explicitly framed the tension between linear storytelling and player agency, motivating architectures that adapt to player actions</cite> <cite id="39de8573-4">Balancing agency with plot often requires hybrid mechanics (e.g., triggerwords) so exploration remains coherent even under freedom</cite>.
- To enable emergent or interpreted narratives without collapsing them: If a player-driven action subverts a character’s role or reveals hidden knowledge, a consistent refusal to adapt can force the player into contrived “correct” paths. Temporarily relaxing consistency allows the player’s interpretation to have weight, then reassert constraints through authorial framing to keep the broader story legible. <cite id="39de8573-3">Emergent narratives arise from player interaction and can be interpreted in diverse ways; developers use narrative mechanics (cutscenes, dialogue) to shape both embedded and emergent stories</cite> <cite id="39de8573-1">Later models connected narrative to agency-supporting architectures</cite>.
- When the player’s agency is threatened by “agency-proof” consistency: In cases where the only way to achieve a player’s stated intention is to have a character contradict their known goals or knowledge, allow a situational exception (e.g., a spy acting on orders, a cursed oath temporarily suspended) so the player can pursue consequentialist aims. <cite id="e534b49a-1">Persona consistency and narrative coherence can conflict; a character who loves travel might be rendered implausible if forced into a road trip during an exam arc. A joint planner can choose among options that respect either constraint</cite> <cite id="e534b49a-1">Sustaining believable interactions requires persona architectures that maintain consistency, but ensuring narrative logic may demand temporary accommodations</cite>.
- To protect moral salience and player identity projection: If a player’s deep identification with a PC or ally makes a consistent refusal to act crush their felt agency, allow the character to yield a small, narratively justified inconsistency (e.g., an ally who “normally” obeys orders disobeys to protect the player’s plan). Title: A Survey on Large Language Model-Based Game Agents
Snippet: Role-playing games (RPGs) require players to assume pre-defined characters with distinct abilities, knowledge, experiences, and objectives. Although RPGs may also incorporate elements of action or adventure, our focus here is on a common characteristic that underpins this genre: role fidelity. Role fidelity means that agents should internalize their assigned role and generate dialogue and actions that remain consistent with the character's identity and capabilities. Failure to do so causes agents to lose consistency in speech and action, or even contradict their assigned role, undermining both immersion and gameplay effectiveness. 

Environments. Social deduction board games provide natural testbeds for role fidelity. In Werewolf, each player receives a hidden role such as seer, guard, or werewolf, and must preserve secrecy while engaging in persuasion, deception, and coordinated voting [174]. Similarly, Avalon assigns asymmetric roles with private knowledge (e.g., Merlin knowing the bad team), requiring agents to participate in multi-round discussions without revealing confidential information while still influencing team decisions [88]. Negotiation games like Diplomacy, where each player embodies a nation with its own objectives [42], and scripted murder-mystery games such as Jubensha [168], reinforce the same demand: agents must consistently inhabit a pre-defined persona and objectives, balancing what to disclose and what to withhold across multiple turns to preserve immersion and effectiveness. 

Classic RPGs also emphasize role fidelity through long-horizon progression. For example, in Pokémon Red, the trainer role requires remembering the current storyline position, the Pokémon owned, the items carried, and the towns and paths visited. PokéAgent introduces exploration tasks to test whether agents can remain coherent as trainers throughout the gameplay [76]. Beyond the main character, role fidelity is even more critical for non-player characters (NPCs), which must sustain consistent personas across repeated interactions and emergent narratives, as exemplified by recent studies evaluating personality fidelity in role-playing [161]. 

Methods. The simplest approach adds the role card directly into the prompt, listing traits and goals as initial memory [109]. While this establishes in-character openings, it quickly breaks down over multi-turn play, i.e., the role drift problem.

Title: Breaking Players’ Expectations: The Role of Non-Player Characters’ Coherence and Consistency
Snippet: N video games, human players control a main character who interacts with non-player characters (NPCs) who populate the game. NPCs are designed with specific characteristics, chosen by game designers, that communicate their role in the narrative. NPCs can play different roles, such as allies or enemies. Game designers often use two characteristics to communicate NPCs' roles in the narrative: appearance and behaviors [1]. Players then form expectations about the role of NPCs based on the perceived coherence between their appearance and their behaviors [2]. Coherence refers to the correspondence between NPCs' features and players' stereotypes. It allows players to understand NPCs' behaviors within the wider context of the game world [3]. Players' expectations are reinforced by the consistency of NPCs' design throughout the game [4]. Consistency refers to the design parameters' alignment, such as appearance and behaviors, over time. It allows players to form expectations and ensure that NPCs' actions match predefined visual cues, in order to convey their role in the game [1]. For example, in a military shooter game, encountering an aggressive NPC who looks like a soldier influences the expectation of hostility when encountering a second NPC with a similar appearance. If the second soldier encountered confirms players' expectations, this will make it easier to predict hostility in subsequent encounters. The aim of maintaining both consistency and coherence between appearance and behaviors is to allow players to form accurate expectations of enemies or allies and, as a result, to improve the overall experience of the game [5]. In particular, when NPCs' behaviors match their appearance and fit logically into the game world, players can better immerse themselves in the narrative and make informed decisions throughout the game. 

As part of their immersion, players form impressions of the NPCs based on their appearance and behaviors [6]. When interacting with NPCs, players assess their perceived intelligence and believability. Perceived intelligence is defined as the player's evaluation of NPCs' abilities to achieve their objective in the narrative, encompassing two dimensions: behaviors' understandability and performance [7].

Snippet: Interactive vignettes foster audience engagement by enabling exploration and influence over narrative progression [44], but they also require narratives to respond dynamically to player interactions while maintaining coherence [4,76]. Because authors are absent during play, they must predefine structures that anticipate diverse interactions, often through multi-branch storytelling. Kumaran et al.
